activities.caption: guess the magnitude — field inside a solenoid
activities.name: emSolenoidEst

config.prompt: A solenoid of 500 turns over 10 cm (n = 5,000 per metre) carries 2 A. What is the field B inside (B = μ₀nI, μ₀ = 4π × 10⁻⁷)?
config.why: B = μ₀nI ≈ 0.0126 T — some 250 times Earth's ~50 μT, from a coil you could hold.
config.context: Earth's surface field is about 50 μT; the solenoid multiplies it 250-fold with a car battery's worth of current.

activities.anchor: Earth's geographic North Pole is a magnetic north pole
activities.caption: find the faulty line in this student's magnet notes
activities.name: emPoleSpot

config.prompt: One line of this student's magnet notes is wrong — click it:
lines: A compass needle's north tip is attracted toward the Arctic.
Unlike poles attract, so the pole up there must be a magnetic south pole.
Cutting a bar magnet in two isolates a monopole — a single free north pole.
Physicists often call the Arctic one the 'north magnetic pole' purely by location, which keeps the confusion alive.
Outside the Earth the field lines run south, closing the loop through the planet's core, where the dynamo lives.
config.correction: You get two weaker dipoles: magnetic field lines always close on themselves, with no free ends — that everyday observation is half of Maxwell's magnetic Gauss law.
config.why: There are no isolated poles — the net flux through any closed surface is zero.

activities.caption: fill the blanks — the household energy ledger
activities.name: emKwhCloze

config.text: One kilowatt-hour is %%0%% joules — so a 2 kW heater run for 3 hours consumes %%1%% kWh. A 10 W LED left on all year burns 87.6 kWh where a 60 W incandescent burned 526 kWh — a factor-of-six saving hiding in P = VI.

activities.anchor: current is used up as it goes round a circuit
activities.caption: file each quantity — same everywhere, or drops en route
activities.name: emCurrentSort

config.prompt: Around a series loop — file each quantity:
buckets: the same everywhere in the loop

items.label: the current returning to the battery

config.why: Charge is conserved: the current leaving equals the current returning, always. Every 'parallel resistors share current equally' error starts here.

config.root: A 12 V battery with 0.05 Ω internal resistance drives a 1.95 Ω load. Walk the calculation.

start.text: First: what total resistance does the loop current see?

choices.label: 1.95 Ω — the internal resistance is negligible
2.0 Ω — internal resistance in series with the load

ideal.text: Kirchhoff's voltage law still holds — but this prediction ignores where 0.3 V of the loop's drop actually lands: inside the battery itself.

real.text: I = 12/2.0 = 6 A, and the terminal voltage sags to 12 − 6 × 0.05 = 11.7 V — the missing 0.3 V heats the battery itself. That single calculation is why car batteries are specified by cold-cranking current and why jump leads are thick copper.

config.why: 'Ideal' is the first word of every circuit theory exam question — real batteries add the productive wrinkle of internal resistance.

activities.caption: pair each safety device with its physics
activities.name: emSafetyMatch

config.prompt: Every rule is physics, not bureaucracy — pair each device with its theorem:

pairs.left: the RCD (trips at 30 mA in ~30 ms)
pairs.right: compares live and neutral currents — which Kirchhoff's law says must be equal — and breaks the instant they differ
encodes I²R heating: twice the rated current makes four times the heat, and the fuse melts first by design
a low-resistance alternative path that keeps a fault's chassis near earth potential — the fault trips the breaker instead of waiting for a hand

pairs.left: 30 mA of AC across the chest
pairs.right: roughly the threshold for ventricular fibrillation — the number the whole design revolves around

config.why: Each device is a conservation law pointed at danger — a theorem applied before breakfast.

config.prompt: From discovery to grid — put the chain in order:
items: Faraday, 1831: a changing magnetic field induces a voltage — no change, no voltage, however strong the magnet
The generator: a coil rotated in a field sees continuously changing flux — alternating voltage, spun by steam, water or wind
The motor: the mirror image — a current-carrying wire in a field feels F = BIL, which turns the axle
The transformer: AC in the primary makes a changing flux in the iron core; Vs/Vp = Ns/Np
The grid: transmit at high voltage and low current — losses are I²R, so raising voltage 100-fold cuts losses 10,000-fold
config.why: The world's electricity is one loop, spun by steam, water or wind — and the grid's whole trick is the transformer's inversion: voltage up, current down.

activities.anchor: a transformer changes DC too, or works without a load
activities.caption: bet before you read on — DC into the primary
activities.name: emDcPredict

config.q: You feed steady DC to a transformer's primary (after the switch-on blip). What does the secondary deliver?
choices: A steady DC voltage, scaled by the turns ratio
Nothing — no changing flux, no induced voltage beyond the switch-on blip
An inverted DC voltage of the same size
The correct ratio, but at half the power
config.why: A transformer needs a changing flux — and with no load on the secondary, almost no current flows in the primary: 'transformers are lazy until loaded' is Faraday's law, not a defect.
